name: Plain Language Summaries for Families
title: Plain Language Summaries for Families
answer: A plain language summary turns the key parts of an IEP into a short explanation families can actually understand, covering goals, services, classroom supports, and who to contact with questions. It matters because IEP documents are long and full of jargon, and many parents leave meetings unsure what was decided for their child. The summary is a bridge to understanding, never a replacement for the IEP or the family's rights to it.

sections.body: An IEP is a long and technical document written in specialist language, and parents often finish meetings without a clear picture of what was decided or what it means for their child. A plain language summary addresses that gap by restating the essential parts of the plan in everyday words. It focuses on the child's goals, the services they will receive, the supports provided in class, and the person to call with questions. The summary exists to build understanding, not to stand in for the formal document. It gives families a usable starting point for conversations with the school.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A teacher can use an approved tool to draft the summary, removing names before the material goes into the tool. The summary should cover the child's goals, services, in-class supports, and the contact for questions, and it can be translated into the family's language and sent through TalkingPoints. Before anything is shared, the teacher checks every summary against the actual IEP, because an error could mislead a family about their child's rights and services. Translations of something this important should be reviewed by a fluent person. When the summary is shared, the teacher should state clearly that it does not replace the IEP or the family's rights to the full document and to explanations from the team.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. Its case is built on the observed experience that IEP documents are long, technical, and full of jargon, and that many parents leave meetings unsure what was decided or what it means for their child. The recommended safeguards, such as checking each summary against the actual IEP and having a fluent person review translations, follow from that practical concern rather than from cited findings.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A summary must never be treated as a substitute for the IEP or for the family's rights to it. Parents are entitled to the full document and to explanations from the team, and the teacher should say plainly when sharing a summary that it is a bridge to understanding rather than a replacement. Every summary has to be checked against the actual IEP, since an error could mislead a family about their child's rights and services. Translations of anything this important should be reviewed by a fluent person. The judgment about what the document means and what the family is entitled to stays with the people on the team, not with the tool.
